ISOLATED HYPERTROPHY OF THE TIBIALIS
ANTERIOR MUSCLE IN THE STIFF LEG
SYNDROME
A 63-year-old woman with a medic al history of insulin-
dependent diabetes mellitus and pernicious anemia
presented with progressive continous stiffness and superim-
posed painful spasms in the left leg for 3 years. Her symp-
toms were often triggered by su dden auditory and tactile
stimuli or by emotional stress. These symptoms resulted in
walking difﬁculties and limitations in daily activities.
Clinical examination showed abnormal posturing of
the left ankle. It was slightly dorsiﬂexed, and active and
passive ankle movements were severely limited due to
associated pain. There was striking isolated hypertrophy
of the left tibialis anterior muscle. There were no signs
of truncal rigidity or lumbar hyperlordosis.
Brain and spinal MRI were normal. EMG showed a typ-
ical pattern of continuous low-frequency ﬁring of normal
motor unit potentials indistinguishable from voluntary
muscle contraction in the tibialis anterior muscle, without
concomitant antagonist muscle activation, despite attempts
at muscle relaxation by the patient. Sudden auditory and
tactile stimuli could not provoke muscle spasms during
EMG examination. EMG of the abdominal, paraspinal,
and other limb muscles showed no abnormalities. Because
stiff leg syndrome was suspect ed, antiglutamic acid decar-
boxylase (GAD) antibodies were assayed and found to be
highly increased (>2000 U/ml; normal <5 U/ml). Insulin
and islet cell antibodies were not measured.
MRI of the lower limbs conﬁrmed isolated hypertro-
phy of the tibialis anterior muscle (Fig. 1). Cerebrospi-
nal ﬂuid (CSF) analysis was normal, and there were no
oligoclonal bands. Diazepam 5 mg twice daily and
monthly intravenous immunoglobulin infusions led to
signiﬁcant clinical improvement. A diagnosis of stiff leg
syndrome was made.
To the best of our knowledge, muscle hypertrophy has
never been described in the stiff person or stiff leg syn-
drome. Several cases of stiff person syndrome were
reported with symptoms conﬁned to one (most often dis-
tal) limb, usually the lower leg.
1,2 The spasms are sponta-
neous, reﬂex-induced, or induced by voluntary movement,
in the absence of truncal rigidity or exaggerated lumbar
lordosis. In contrast to the typical stiff person syndrome,
serum/CSF anti-GAD antibodies and oligoclonal bands in
the CSF are most often absent in the stiff limb syndrome,
making a deﬁnitive diagnosis sometimes difﬁcult.
3
Isolated tibialis anterior muscle hypertrophy in our
patient seemed to be related to persistent muscle con-
traction, as has been seen in other muscle disorders
associated with involuntary muscle contraction (e.g.,
myotonic syndromes, rippling muscle syndrome, and
dystonia).

Anaesthetic management
of a patient with Stiff–person
syndrome
Stiff–person syndrome (SPS) is a rare
disease characterised by muscle rigidity
and episodic spasms in the trunk and
extre-mities. We report the anaesthet-
ic management of three operations in a
SPS patient.
A 40-year-old female with invasive
thymoma was scheduled for thymecto-
my. She had been diagnosed as SPS based
on her symptoms of constant stiffness in
the legs and trunk accompanied by
episodic painful spasms. Auto-antibody
against glutamic acid decarboxylase
(GAD) was detected in her serum. After
induction with fentanyl 2 lg.kg
)1, thi-
opental 3 mg.kg )1 and vecuronium
8 mg, anaesthesia was maintained with
isoﬂurane 0.4–1%, nitrous oxide, addi-
tional fentanyl and vecuronium. Soon
after the operation, she was fully awake
and train-of-four ratio monitored in the
ulnar nerve recovered to 100%.
Six weeks later, the patient under-
went an emergency appendectomy.
Anaesthesia was induced and maintained
with diazepam 5 mg, fentanyl 4 lg.kg
–l,
thiopental 3 mg.kg )1, vecuronium
13 mg in total, isoﬂurane 0.8–1.5%,
and nitrous oxide.
The following year, she was sched-
uled for endoscopic nasal sinus surgery.
Anaesthesia was induced with fentanyl
2 lg.kg
)1, propofol 10 mg.kg )1.h)1,
vecuronium 0.8 mg.kg )1 and main-
tained with propofol 3–4 mg.kg )1.h)1,
nitrous oxide and additional fentanyl.
The patient regained 25% T 1 twitch
30 min after the initial dose of vecuro-
nium. Additional doses of vecuronium
1.5 mg were administered at about
30-min intervals. In the three operations,
haemodynamic parameters were rela-
tively stable and the patient awakened
soon after anaesthesia. Symptoms of
muscle rigidity and spasms temporarily
improved after each anaesthesia.
Auto-antibody against GAD, the
enzyme essential for GABA production,
is detected in 90% of SPS patients [1] and
autoimmune pathogenesis has been
strongly suggested in this disease [2, 3].
Loss of GABA-ergic inhibitory regula-
tion on spinal and supraspinal [4] motor
neurones may possibly result in sponta-
neous ﬁring of motor units, leading
to muscle rigidity or episodic spasms.
Although isoﬂurane and propofol exert
theiranaestheticeffectsthroughenhance-
ment of GABA-ergic inhibition, they did
not seem to have altered anaesthetic
effects in our SPS patient, suggesting that
control of the sensory system is relatively
preserved in this disease. Temporary
improvement of muscle rigidity and
spasms after each anaesthetic was possibly
caused by residual effect of isoﬂurane and
propofol on motor units. Concerning
neuromuscular blocking drugs, 25%
twitch recovery time for vecuronium
was within normal range in our patient,
indicating that the neuromuscular junc-
tion is not affected in this disease.
In summary, in contrast with a case
report describing prolonged hypotonic-
ity after general anaesthesia in SPS [5],
the effects of general anaesthesia or
neuromuscular blocking drug were not
altered in our SPS patient.
